subject: WSJ Travel: Even More Quirky Travel Hacks 😁
body_text:
96 Plus, a big vacation merger and New York-Australia nonstop   Is this email difficult to read? View in browser                 Dawn Gilbertson   Travel Hacks and More Travel Hacks   Plus, a big vacation merger and New York-Australia nonstop   Happy Friday and goodbye (almost) to September! Hope you’re keeping a close eye on your flight status if you’re traveling to or from the East Coast this weekend given the forecasted Nor’easter. Check your airline’s website or app for any waivers to change your flight without the usual penalties. Do it before everyone else does and you’ll have more options. 

   If travel turns out to be a mess, the week will end the way it started, with major flight woes due to an air-traffic control issue . 

   In other travel news this week, Royal Caribbean said it is buying a 50% stake in Caribbean all-inclusive resort operator Sandals. Get ready for more Sandals and Beaches resorts, the executives say, but not day passes to the resorts on a cruise stop. 

   Qantas said its long-awaited nonstop service between Sydney and New York will begin in mid-2028 . Tickets for the 18-hour flight are expected to go on sale in August. The airline is launching Sydney-London flights, the first phase of its Project Sunrise project, in October 2027. 

   And luxury cruise-ship operator Explora Journeys is the latest to expand into river cruising. The company announced a deal for five ships. Reservations won’t begin until sometime next year. 

       Readers share their travel hacks     Chug a beer before braving security? It helps one reader. SPENCER PLATT/GETTY IMAGES   Who doesn’t love a good travel shortcut, packing tip or money-saving move?

   I shared some new-to-me travel hacks in early September after scrolling through the responses to a Threads post and asked you to chime in with your favorites. They’re still coming in! 

   The one that made me laugh out loud came from Patrick Nowicki in Denmark. “I always take a cold can of beer (or one for each traveler) and drink it just before security. It costs 10% of an airport beer and removes much of the ‘security check stress.’”

   Check out some of the others: 

   Book one parent in business class . “My wife and I took our three kids (8, 7 and 1) to Europe this summer for our 10th wedding anniversary. We dreaded the red-eye flight from Seattle to London with a baby. Rather than buy the one-year-old a seat in economy it was roughly the same to book my wife in business class. We let him get the craziness out with me in coach, then I brought him up to her after he fell asleep. Both of them slept until we landed. Wife happy, baby happy, boom!” —Ethan Bays, Oregon

   Turn to AI to brush up on foreign languages . “My wife and I were in the Provence region of France last year. My high school French was very rusty so I used Claude to create a one-pager of key phrases, which was very helpful to prepare for the trip. I like to be able to say a few words in the local language.” —Charles Vianey, Alabama

   Carry on a seat cushion. “Those inexpensive inflatable seat cushions make travel in economy bearable, if not comfortable. The new aircraft seats are poorly padded, especially for older folks. Living in Hawaii, trips to Europe have a combined travel time of 16+ hours, and flights to the mainland U.S. are over five hours. My wife and I find that these cushions are indispensable.” —Lance Fujisaki, Hawaii

   Put those sandwich baggies to good use at the airport . “Keep a small ziplock bag in your pocket. You never know what flotsam and jetsam collects in your pocket before a flight, and this is the easiest way to gather it and drop it into your carry-on at security.” —Dan Waldman, New York

   Power up with an international adapter . “As someone who gets to airline status the long way, here’s my favorite: Bring an international plug adapter even when flying domestically. The domestic outlets in planes are often worn out and your chargers won’t work or they slip out. The international ports get used less frequently so sometimes you can get power when you otherwise wouldn’t be able to.” —Robert Book, Texas

   Skip the in-flight movie and get organized . “Use your idle time on a plane to cull your redundant and unwanted photos in your phone’s photo library, and to set up albums of photos from specific trips and events.” —Dave Kamer, Kentucky

   BYOHP : “If you get freezing cold like I do, or your back aches from uncomfortable seats, bring your own heating pad and plug it in at your seat. It’s especially great for long flights in lie-flat beds.” —Jennifer Smith, Texas

   Look for the hidden seat button. “The aisle armrest seems locked down but on every one there is a hidden button at the base which you can push to lift up. It makes getting in and out a bit easier, especially when you’ve got little kids.” —Nicholas Conant, Illinois (a former pilot)

   Repurpose that hotel room ironing board. “I use the ironing board as a place to put hangers to dry wet gym clothes and delicates as most rooms have few hooks. I also use the ironing board to store my books, spare electronics and papers, especially when sharing a room.” —Lynn Exton, New York

   Pack a thumb drive with backup documents on big trips . “I make digital copies of passports and travel and contact information and keep them on a thumb drive. We actually each carry one with us in case, God forbid, something happens and we can’t speak. The authorities would find the thumb drive and be able to more quickly reach out to our emergency contacts or the embassy.” —John Hester, Georgia

   This is an edition of the WSJ Travel newsletter, a weekly source of inspiration and advice for navigating your vacations and business trips, along with the latest travel news. If you’re not subscribed, sign up here . 

       Notes From the Road ✈️     PETER ARKLE FOR WSJ   • You, too, can be whisked through the airport like a VIP—for a hefty fee. I tested three airline services . 

   • Insulated bags, hotel-freezer favors and strategic packing: the trick to getting artisanal butter home from Paris .

   • Did you get a deal at Disney parks this year? Price cuts and promotions helped boost attendance as rivals slumped.

   • Surfers can’t get enough of the epic swells in Newport Beach, hazards and all .

       One Good Tip 🎯   Don’t book a hotel room with points and forget about it until check-in. Keep searching on the chain’s website or app to see if a better deal pops up, and rebook if there are no penalties. Similarly, don’t give up on that hotel at the top of your list just because it’s showing no points availability. Someone might cancel or more rooms might open up in this era of dynamic pricing. I found a coveted hotel reservation for an Aruba trip during a 1 a.m. bout of insomnia this week.

       Travel Math 🧮   $179.30   The average daily hotel rate in the U.S. for the week ending Sept. 19. That was up 5.7% from a year earlier and the highest on record, according to CoStar. (The figures aren’t inflation-adjusted.)

       And We Quote 💬   “Never say never, but I don’t think the effort to erase my time as CEO is very consistent with me wanting to go back on ‘It’s a Small World.’” 

   —Former Disney CEO Bob Chapek, who says he hasn’t been back to Walt Disney World since his high-profile ouster in 2022. He has no plans to go despite being a lifelong fan of the parks.

       You Have Thoughts 🤔   …on airline lost-and-found : 

   • “My wife and kids flew back from Singapore into Newark recently on Singapore Airlines. In baggage claim, my daughter realized that she left her Kindle onboard. I got a panicked call from my wife as I was driving to pick them up. I typed, ‘I left my Kindle on a Singapore Airlines flight at EWR. Who should I call?’ and Gemini turned up a number. A human being answered, who then called the gate agent. They found the Kindle, called me back and told me to tell my wife to stay at the baggage claim area where they would bring the Kindle. All resolved right then and there. Felt like a miracle.” — Gary Lin, New York 

   • “I left a small bag with my power adapters and cables in the side pocket on my British Airways flight. Not the end of the world, but those things add up. I realized it on the airport bus and returned to the terminal at LAX. I confess my expectations were low that I would see this again. I couldn’t have been more wrong. The staff called the gate, where the cleaning crew had already found the item. I was told it would take a bit of time to get it through customs, but was invited to sit and wait. Sure enough, within 20 minutes I got it back: no hassle, no form, no fee, no remote location—just a simple handover.” — Alex Johnson, California  

   …on travel tips : 

   • “The advice from your recent column was to leave your umbrella at home and pick one up as needed. This might be good advice for a light sprinkle in Florence, but last night I arrived at Tokyo Central Station during a typhoon and was happy to zip open my carry-on and take out my umbrella.” — Michael West, Wisconsin 

   (Responses have been condensed and edited.)
